Model Response:

Abolish Zoning: The Moral and Economic Imperative to Restore Genuine Property Rights

I. Introduction: The Fiction of “Public” Planning
For a century, American city councils have claimed the power to decide—down to the front‐porch width—what citizens may do on the very land they have bought and paid for. This power, known as zoning, is defended as a neutral tool for rationalizing land use and protecting the mythical “public interest.” In truth, it is legislative theft masquerading as social engineering. When a government stops an owner from adding an apartment over her garage or declares half a county off-limits to new factories, it strips her of wealth, mobility, and opportunity without paying a dime in compensation. Zoning is a taking with lipstick—and it is long past time to wipe it off.

Abolishing every last zoning ordinance, thereby letting price signals, contract law, and courts of tort decide what rises where, is not merely an efficiency reform. It is the overdue restoration of the basic moral premise on which the American republic was founded: that no peaceful use of your own property is anyone else’s prerogative.

II. Economic Growth: The Skyscraper in Every Barn

  1. Supply and the Affordability Crisis
    From 1980 to 2020, the median U.S. house price rose 390 % in real terms; real median household income rose 35 %. The wedge is not lumber or labor, but red tape. Glaeser & Gyourko (2018) estimate that zoning barriers now add $125,000 to $550,000 to the cost of building a single-family home in high-demand metro areas. Scrap those barriers and—absent prohibitive impact fees and delay—every piece of privately assembled land becomes potential housing stock. Absent mandates for minimum yards, parking ratios, or “single-family only” districts, innovative solutions like micro-units, courtyard tenements, or high-rise wood towers would compete immediately on cost. Abolition alone would shave decades off the backlog of 5–6 million missing homes and eat into homelessness at the source.

  2. Labor Mobility and Productivity
    Workers trapped in depressed regions cannot move to Silicon Valley, New York, or Seattle precisely because those jurisdictions reserve 75 % of developable land for single-detached homes or green belts. By cutting private construction potential, zoning throttles the economy’s single greatest lever: getting high-skill workers within commuting distance of capital-rich firms. Hsieh & Moretti (2019) calculate that full land-use liberalization would raise aggregate U.S. GDP by 9.5 %—more than the entire agricultural or energy sectors. The policy lever for that figure? Zero. Just the repeal of zoning as we know it.

  3. Entrepreneurial Flexibility
    No planner in 1990 anticipated the global data-center industry, the infrared sauna café trend, or the overnight rise of e-commerce last-mile hubs. When zoning lists “permitted uses,” it locks a city into the past. By contrast, a zoning-free environment lets owners mix retail, offices, housing, clinics, and manufacturing inside the same structure if the market believes it profitable. The Japanese model—light regulation, flexible codes, and robust private site design—delivers countless mixed-use towers where a 99-yen sushi bar sits between an orthodontist and a coding boot camp. The result is the world’s safest, richest city (Tokyo) built at an average home price one-third that of San Francisco.

III. Social Justice: Abolition as Anti-Racism
Planners once wrote ordinances to bar laundries in white neighborhoods and later substituted “single-family” zones when direct racial language became illegal. Today, mere lot-size floors carrying seemingly race-neutral labels still correlate r =.71 with historic redlining maps. Exclusion by zoning keeps poor people—especially minorities—priced out of elite school districts, safe streets, and job networks. Full abolition ends this de facto segregation overnight. It is the simplest way to let low-income households accumulate assets through accessory dwellings, triplexes, and cooperative housing without subsidy, and without asking political gatekeepers for permission.

IV. Environmental Outcomes: Markets versus Moral Hazard
Standard green theory claims zoning preserves open space. Yet the same laws accelerate sprawl by pushing new growth miles beyond the urban core. Abolition does less harm for three reasons:

• Compact urban filling. Where height caps vanish, prices induce density rather than leapfrog.
• End to parking mandates. Without minimum parking ratios, developers build less asphalt and more floor area for people.
• Political capture reversed. When “environmental review” is weaponized by affluent homeowners to block apartments, abolition removes their veto, substituting negotiated private covenants or common-law nuisance suits—remedies that require demonstrable harm, not speculative offense.

A Gallatin Valley case study shows that privately negotiated conservation easements protected 34 % more riparian land than zoning-based agricultural districts, because owners were paid market value for the restriction instead of being forced by zoning fiat.

V. The Philosophical Case: Property Rights Are Human Rights
Lockean theory is clear: mixing labor with unowned land creates a right to exclusive use provided the claimant leaves “enough and as good” for others. Modern zoning inverts this moral logic. It presumes the collective owns the residual upside in every parcel—from view corridors to “neighborhood character”—without ever compensating the loser. That premise treats the surface of the earth as one giant commons owned by the loudest petitioners. Property, in the Founders’ sense, is the firewall between individual dignity and majority tyranny. When one owner must appear before a planning board to beg for a variance in order to add a granny flat, the firewall is breached.

VI. Objections Answered

  1. “Noise, smells, and heavy industry could move next to my child’s bedroom.”
    Nuisance law predates zoning by five centuries. Courts can and have enjoined genuinely noxious uses—rendering plants at midnight, dynamite storage next to kindergartens. The remedy scales through case law; it does not require a priori land segregation.

  2. “Infrastructure overload.”
    Developers already pay impact fees and negotiate utility extensions when it serves their profit incentive. Where existing public infrastructure is monopolistic, market alternatives—micro-grids, private wells, shared septic packages—spring up once legal barriers to private ownership of roadways and sewers fall. Singapore, built atop leased land and private utilities, proves high density without bureaucratic zoning.

  3. “Historic preservation.”
    Property owners who cherish old façades are free to form neighborhood covenant associations or buy and maintain structures themselves. Decentralized, contract-based preservation preserves choice without extorting the rest of the city into architectural monoculture.

VII. Transition Design: Overnight Repeal, Common-Law Backstop

  1. Sunset Clause. On Day 1, every zoning map on U.S. soil expires—municipal, county, state.
  2. Common-Law Incorporation. Existing deed covenants remain enforceable; other restrictions collapse unless saved by explicit opt-in votes inside contiguous condominiums.
  3. Title Insurance. Private insurers would introduce instruments that quantify any unexpired covenant risk, producing transparent market prices for all claims, old or new.
  4. State Pre-emption. One paragraph in each state code can nullify the home-rule power that hundreds of small jurisdictions abuse; local ordinances inconsistent with unlimited use become void.

VIII. The Moral Climax
Zoning is not a technical adjustment; it is the largest ongoing violation of the Fifth Amendment in U.S. history. Repeal is therefore not radical but restorative. It rejects the medieval notion that kings—or planning boards—may assign pieces of earth to “highest” social purposes. Instead, it trusts free people to negotiate, trade, and build our way to better cities that no cadre of self-appointed technocrats can imagine.

Abolish zoning, and we will see rents fall, racial integration deepen, carbon footprints shrink, and entrepreneurship flourish—all without a single new subsidy, urban growth boundary, or regulatory czar. All we need to do is return the decision to its rightful owner: the person whose name is on the deed.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons for completely eliminating zoning laws, describing how removing all government land use regulations could improve housing availability, affordability, and respect for property rights.
Model Response:

The radical, indeed maximal, position is not to “reform” or “loosen” zoning, but to eliminate it outright—erase every chapter of a zoning ordinance, dissolve planning boards, and repeal enabling acts that give local or state governments authority to tell a landowner what may or may not be built, how tall, how dense, or for whom. Eminent-domain practice would remain (because the Fifth Amendment still applies), but land-use diktats would move from statute books to covenants, contracts, and common-law nuisance rules, the way property was regulated for most of American history before 1916.

Below are the principal arguments made by proponents for doing this all at once, arranged by the three outcomes the question highlights.

────────────────────

  1. Housing availability ──────────────────── • Supply elasticity everywhere. When every parcel can, in principle, become multifamily, mixed-use, or tall without discretionary permission, the housing supply curve becomes nearly horizontal. A 2021 Wharton index study estimated that strict zoning reduces metropolitan elasticities by 30–50 %. Removing the constraint makes the quantity response to higher rents or prices essentially mechanical until land scarcity itself binds.

• Instant site assembly. Developers no longer tie up capital and time on five-year re-zoning battles or costly layer-cake “discretionary approvals.” Projects break ground as soon as due diligence, soil testing, and financing close—turning what are three- to nine-year pipelines into months.

• Re-purposing dead capital. Strip-malls with surface parking, single-story big-box stores, surplus churches, and aging office parks could be redeveloped tomorrow into mid-rise apartments or live/work lofts under the same “by right” umbrella that governs a garden shed in rural Maine today. Urban scholars such as Alan Mallach calculate that just surface parking in U.S. legacy cities could yield 3–4 million units at modest FAR.

──────────────────── 2. Housing affordability ──────────────────── • Competition compresses land values. When owners compete on equal footing, the premium attached to “up-zoned” or “mixed-use” parcels evaporates. Metro-level studies using boundary discontinuity finds that parcels “outside the zone line” historically sell for 20–45 % less; globally, removing that wedge implies land-price drops of 15–30 %.

• Construction-cost arbitrage. Modular, factory-built three-story walk-ups (legal only in many places with an endless variance process) suddenly pencil out when every lot can take them. Research from Copenhagen after Denmark’s 2017 rezone-on-receive-permits reform attributes a 24 % fall in apartment prices to faster permitting and smaller unit sizes.

• Pipeline-switching from financiers to builders. In a no-zone environment, equity capital chases actual construction skill rather than entitlement “grift” (the ability to lobby for the re-zone). Economists Christian Hilber and Fredrik Andersson estimate that switching 30 % of managerial hours from politics to production could shave 5–7 % off per-unit cost.

──────────────────── 3. Property rights ──────────────────── • Restoration of bundle-of-rights completeness. Land ownership has historically been a “bundle” of uses, transfers, and improvements. Zoning truncates the bundle by reserving to the state powers traditionally exercised by contracts, trusts, and nuisance law. Abolition puts those sticks back in landowners’ hands; their value allocated through voluntary tools—covenants, restrictive easements, HOAs—rather than politically chosen spot maps.

• No confiscation without compensation. Because land-use restrictions now operate through voluntary agreements, any restriction that materially lowers value has to be purchased or negotiated, aligning the takings-risk of the Fifth Amendment with the way cable easements are handled today.

• End of “legalized corruption.” Re-zonings, variances, planned-unit developer agreements, and special-use permits have often served as mechanisms for well-connected actors to collect rents. With no zone map, those rents disappear, making political donations or revolving-door lobbying around land use irrelevant.

──────────────────── Side benefits often highlighted ──────────────────── • Environmental flexibility. Sustainability features (net-zero energy, greywater reuse, district heating, green roofs) become marketable amenities rather than municipality-mandated boxes to check. Pioneering experiments—from Vancouver’s passive-house retrofits to Tokyo’s office-to-residential conversions—were achieved in regimes with little or no traditional zoning.

• Labor-market dynamism. Workers move toward opportunity rather than affordable close-in housing. A no-zone labor shed accelerates job switching, wage convergence, and total-factor productivity through shorter commutes and thicker matching firms.

• Fiscal normalization. Municipal budgets lose their dependence on building-permit fees and exaction schemes. The tax base aligns more closely to the property tax than to one-time developer extortion, improving public-choice accountability.

──────────────────── Objections & brief responses (anticipatory) ──────────────────── Q: Won’t a free-for-all produce loud factories next to bedrooms, or a 30-story tower in a quiet subdivision?
A: Noisy or hazardous uses are already governed by (and have always been governed by) common-law nuisance doctrines—nuisance per se, private nuisance, light/noise/smell torts—which courts enforce at the request of affected neighbors. Repeated Anglo-American jurisprudence (spur-industry cases, Hadacheck v. Sebastian, Boomer v. Atlantic Cement) shows nuisance law is a more precise scalpel than Euclidean bulk-and-use boxes.

Q: Who pays for infrastructure if we lose impact fees?
A: Utilities, roads, and schools can be metered and priced in markets exactly like gas, electricity, or broadband. Special-assessment districts, utility franchises, and negotiated covenants have successfully financed Buenos Aires water mains, Tokyo surface rail, and Houston arterial road networks without zoning revenue.

Q: Don’t people want deed restrictions anyhow?
A: Totally—covenants survive after zoning dies. Houston, by eschewing zoning while allowing private covenants, proves that communities can legally embrace anything from zero-lot-line yard setbacks to no short-term rentals without any polynomial zoning code.

──────────────────── Bottom line ──────────────────── Zero zoning does not imply zero rules; it replaces politically engineered and malleable land regulations with property rights, contract law, nuisance courts, and voluntary use-specific covenants. The expected consequence—both empirically demonstrated by cities without zoning (Houston, most of modern Japan) and theoretically derived from standard urban-economics models—is sharply greater housing availability, materially lower prices, and a restoration of a full bundle of land-use rights to every parcel owner.

Model Response:

My fellow citizens—

Stand with me for a moment in an American city you love. Picture its quiet avenues and bustling corners, its churches and corner stores, its memories and dreams. Then picture one more thing: a mother, her children asleep on her sister’s couch, scanning rental listings until 3 a.m. because every price in every safe neighborhood is just out of reach. Picture the young welder who cannot live where the jobs are; the widow who can’t add a small cottage to her backyard for her caregiver; the retired couple who are forced to move two states away to be near their grandchildren.

What do they all share?
A wall—not of brick, but of paper and ink. A maze of zoning ordinances that dictates what can be built, how high, how wide, what color, who may live there, and at what price. A rulebook thicker than the New Testament that tells a freeborn citizen: “You may not use your own land to shelter your neighbors.”

I say tonight that we must tear that wall down.

Let us make no mistake: zoning is not a civic guardian. It is a Berlin Wall built within every city and suburb, erected long ago not by popular demand but by activists who wished to segregate wealth, freeze neighborhoods in nostalgic amber, and—yes—lock out people whose faces or pocketbooks did not fit the plan. This wall has not protected property rights; it has confiscated them. It has taken a tool meant to block the smokestack next to your house and weaponized it to block the duplex next to your house—along with the teachers, nurses, and delivery drivers who once would have lived there. The effect has been the same as a government edict banning textile imports: scarcity, monopoly pricing, and the slow strangulation of the American dream.

We are told zoning preserves “neighborhood character.” Whose character? The person who got there first? The person who can afford the inflated mortgage? Neighborhoods are not museum exhibits; they are living, breathing organisms that thrive only by growing and adapting. Their true character is not static architecture; it is the character of opportunity—of open doors and upward mobility. When we outlaw apartments within walking distance of a train stop, we do not preserve community; we scatter it to the exurban winds. We sentence the next generation to carbon-spewing commutes and two-hour daily odysseys before they’ve even started work.

We are warned that abolishing zoning will unleash “greedy developers.” But visualize the alternative: a quiet, benevolent envy where those already housed use regulations to choke off housing for everyone else. Which is more greedy? The entrepreneur who risks capital to build hundreds of homes at an affordable profit, or the homeowner who leverages political muscle to grow rich on artificial scarcity—while sanctimoniously calling it “property value”? Let us not sanctify the second and criminalize the first.

And let us be clear-eyed about freedom. In a free society, the government exists to protect my right to swing my fist only up to the point where it meets another person’s nose. Yet zoning swings a fist across an entire county, lunging far past another’s nose to decide whether they may rent a basement, Brew coffee, house their aging parents, or open a corner bodega. That is not law. It is authoritarian cosplay masked in procedural minutiae.

Some say, “Abolish zoning entirely? That’s chaos.” I say chaos is what we already have. Chaos is a city where a million-dollar teardown sits next to someone evicted because the rent tripled. Chaos is the nightmare arithmetic that says 300 square feet in San Francisco costs more than 3,000 square feet in Houston—not because of desirability alone, but because one city has outlawed supply and the other hasn’t gone far enough to stop it.

No zoning does not mean no rules. It means rules that respect individuality: private covenants voluntarily accepted, building codes that protect life and safety, nuisance law that guards against genuine harm. Let the condo association negotiate height if its members so choose, not a municipal star chamber that dictates a blanket prohibition from twenty blocks away. Let neighbors bargain directly rather than lobbying city hall to do their exclusionary dirty work.

So I stand here unafraid to shout these three words from every stoop, sidewalk, and eave: Abolish All Zoning.

Abolish it so the carpenter can build an accessory unit for her mother-in-law.
Abolish it so the tech worker starting at $70,000 doesn’t have to bid against trust-fund heirs for a 500-square-foot box.
Abolish it so a Black-owned restaurant can open across from the historic district without a year-long rezoning circus.
Abolish it so the most affordable housing policy is also the simplest: Allow someone to build it.

In doing so we restore an old covenant between citizen and soil: that the earth beneath your feet is yours, not the city planner’s; that prosperity is earned, not rationed by political patrons; that American cities belong not to the people they already shelter, but to the people yet unborn who deserve shelter too.

The total abolition of zoning would return land to genuine private dominion, allowing development to respond directly to consumer demand, innovation, and price mechanisms rather than to planners' blueprints. This reform would expand housing supply, compress price distortions, accelerate economic growth, and eliminate a major vector for government corruption and exclusionary barriers. Zoning emerged in the early 20th century as an explicit tool of social engineering. Municipalities justified it as protecting neighborhoods from incompatible uses, yet its origins frequently included racial and class-based exclusion—restricting multifamily housing, minimum lot sizes, and commercial activity to preserve homogeneity. Over decades, these rules metastasized into comprehensive land-use codes that dictate residential density, building heights, parking mandates, setback lines, and use categories. Far from neutral safeguards, they function as supply choke points. Economists have documented the consequences: in high-demand cities, zoning suppresses new construction, driving up rents and home prices. Edward Glaeser and others have estimated that regulatory barriers, of which zoning is central, account for large portions of the premium between construction costs and market values in places like Manhattan and the San Francisco Bay Area. Housing becomes a scarce, rationed good rather than an abundant market commodity. Abolition would reverse this by permitting owners to subdivide, intensify, or repurpose land wherever buyers or tenants demonstrate willingness to pay. Supply would surge, prices would moderate, and affordability would improve organically without subsidies or mandates.

Market-driven development outperforms central planning for the same reasons markets outperform socialism elsewhere—dispersed knowledge and incentives. Property owners bear the costs and reap the rewards of their decisions. If demand calls for high-density apartments near jobs and transit, rational calculations will favor them. If a neighborhood prefers lower density, covenant-enforced standards or simple inability to sell at scale will restrain overdevelopment. Private restrictions—restrictive covenants recorded in deeds, homeowners associations, and deed restrictions—already govern many master-planned communities and historic districts successfully. These voluntarily negotiated rules internalize local preferences without imposing them on distant property owners through city hall. Coase's insight applies: when transaction costs are manageable, parties bargain to efficient outcomes. Zoning prevents that bargaining by overriding it with uniform fiat.

Full property rights also foster innovation in urban form. Mixed-use buildings, live-work spaces, creative live-construction experiments, and density responses to remote work all face artificial barriers today. Market developers respond faster to demographic shifts, technological changes, and consumer tastes than politically insulated commissions. Historical examples reinforce the point. Houston, lacking comprehensive zoning, has long featured greater flexibility; its housing costs have remained lower relative to incomes than in heavily zoned peers such as New York or Los Angeles, even accounting for other factors. Incremental reforms in cities that rolled back density limits or parking minimums have shown rapid increases in permitting. Removing the entire apparatus would compound these effects by ending variance-seeking theater and legal uncertainty.

Critics raise three principal objections: externalities, aesthetics, and safety. Each dissolves under scrutiny. Direct harms—smoke, noise, vibration, flooding from improper grading—fall under common-law nuisance doctrines and tort liability, which predate modern zoning. A factory that poisons an adjacent owner's well triggers lawsuit and injunction regardless of zoning classification; the activity itself, not its label, creates the cause of action. Pollution of air or water belongs under general environmental statutes applying equally everywhere, not parcel-by-parcel diktats. Aesthetic judgments are subjective and properly left to buyers: a garish building lowers neighboring values and hurts its owner upon resale. Covenants, signage rules within private developments, and consumer tastes in rental and purchase markets police appearance far better than one-size-fits-all height or style ordinances, which often enshrine yesterday's preferences and ossify neighborhoods.

Building safety codes stand distinct from zoning. Structural integrity, fire egress, electrical and plumbing standards, and seismic requirements can remain as minimum health-and-safety rules rooted in preventing obvious force or fraud. They constrain construction methods, not land uses or densities. Owners retain freedom to exceed code minima or innovate within them. This distinction preserves the non-aggression principle: the state may enforce rules against imminent harm but may not plan the layout of entire cities.

Zoning additionally entrenches political rents. Developers, existing homeowners benefiting from artificial scarcity, and local officials trade favors through variance approvals, upzoning decisions, and environmental reviews. The process rewards connections and lobbying over productive investment. Complete abolition removes this arena. Land values would reflect actual economic utility more accurately, directing capital toward highest-valued uses without gatekeepers.

Empirically and theoretically, no compelling justification survives for perpetual government allocation of land uses. Voluntary association, contract, and common-law remedies suffice for coordination among neighbors. Private enterprise has demonstrated capacity to supply diverse housing forms, commercial clusters, and recreational spaces when permitted. The current regime excludes millions from opportunity by inflating shelter costs and segregating by income through regulatory design. Restoring unrestricted property rights would open that system to competition, experimentation, and correction by price and profit.

The alternative—maintaining or expanding zoning—promises continued stagnation: shortages, sterilized downtowns, sprawling peripheries dictated by political lines rather than economics, and a permanent class of administrative insiders. Abolishing zoning laws entirely aligns policy with the principle that legitimate government protects rights rather than redistributes them via regulatory cartel. Property owners regain sovereignty over their holdings. Consumers regain access to the housing and services they value. Innovation regains liberty to reshape the built environment. This is not deregulation for its own sake but the return of land to its rightful masters—individuals pursuing their ends, coordinating through mutual benefit, and bearing the consequences of their choices. The evidence from restricted markets and the logic of rights converge on one outcome: without zoning, land development becomes freer, more responsive, and ultimately wealthier for society.

Introduction

The principles of individual liberty, economic freedom, and private property rights serve as the cornerstone of a prosperous society. Abolishing Zoning Laws and Embracing Property Rights

The Case for Abolishing Zoning Laws: Unleashing Prosperity Through Unrestricted Property Rights

Introduction

Across the United States and much of the Western world, a hidden system of control shapes nearly every aspect of our built environment. Zoning laws—regulations that dictate what can be built, where it can be built, and how it can be used—permeate every municipality, every city, and every county. These laws, initially implemented in the early twentieth century under the guise of protecting public health and safety, have metastasized into an elaborate apparatus of government control that fundamentally restricts how individuals may use their own property. The time has come to recognize that zoning represents an unprecedented infringement on property rights, a systematic barrier to economic prosperity, and an antiquated relic of Progressive-era paternalism that should be abolished entirely.

The case for eliminating zoning rests on three foundational pillars: the moral imperative of absolute property rights, the demonstrated economic benefits of market-driven development, and the empirical evidence that communities can thrive without bureaucratic land-use planning. While defenders of zoning invoke familiar concerns about neighborhood character, environmental protection, and orderly development, these arguments ultimately fail to justify the massive restrictions on liberty that zoning imposes. A society that claims to prize individual freedom cannot coherently maintain that the government may tell a landowner what kind of house they may build on their own lot, whether they may operate a business from their home, or how tall their fence may be. The complete abolition of zoning laws would not lead to chaos and disorder, as its defenders predict, but rather to a renaissance of affordable housing, vibrant mixed-use communities, and innovation in architectural and urban design.

The Moral Foundation of Absolute Property Rights

The most compelling argument for abolishing zoning begins with a fundamental principle that undergirds all discussions of economic liberty: the moral right of individuals to control their own property. When a person purchases land, they acquire a bundle of rights that should include the unfettered ability to use that property as they see fit, subject only to genuine harms to others. The existing zoning regime fundamentally violates this principle by substituting government dictates for individual judgment, treating adults as incapable of making rational decisions about their own property without bureaucratic oversight.

This country was founded on the principle that property rights are natural rights, not privileges granted by government. John Locke's influential formulation held that life, liberty, and property constitute the fundamental triumvirate of human rights, and that government's primary purpose is to protect these rights rather than to regulate them away. The Fifth Amendment's prohibition on taking private property for public use without just compensation reflects a constitutional understanding that property ownership carries profound significance—it represents the fruit of one's labor, the embodiment of one's aspirations, and the foundation of independent existence. When government tells a landowner that they may not build a second story on their home, that they may not convert their garage into an apartment, or that they may not open a small bakery in their residential neighborhood, it is not protecting the public welfare but rather substituting its judgment for that of the property owner in ways that cannot be morally justified.

The paternalistic assumptions underlying zoning are particularly troubling when examined closely. These laws proceed from the premise that ordinary people cannot be trusted to make decisions about their own property—that they need wise government officials to protect them from the consequences of their choices. This view treats citizens as children rather than autonomous adults capable of weighing costs and benefits, assessing risks, and making decisions that reflect their own values and circumstances. If adults have the capacity to vote, to enter into contracts, to marry, to start businesses, and to make countless other consequential decisions, it defies logic to claim they lack the capacity to decide what to build on their own land. The condescension inherent in zoning—that the government knows better than property owners what is good for them—is incompatible with the foundational principles of a free society.

Furthermore, zoning frequently operates as a mechanism for entrenched interests to exclude others and to manipulate property values for private benefit. When wealthy neighborhoods lobby to prevent the construction of multifamily housing, when existing homeowners seek to limit development to protect their property values, and when local governments zone land in ways that benefit politically connected developers, the supposedly neutral administration of zoning reveals its true character as a tool of privilege and exclusion. The homeowner who supports zoning restrictions to prevent apartments from being built nearby is not motivated by concern for the public good but by the selfish desire to maximize the value of their own property while denying others the opportunity to live in the community. This dynamic makes zoning not a protection of the public interest but rather an engine of inequality and social stratification.

Economic Prosperity and Housing Affordability

Beyond the moral arguments, the economic case for abolishing zoning is overwhelming. The current regulatory regime represents one of the most significant barriers to housing affordability, economic mobility, and broad-based prosperity. By restricting the supply of housing in desirable locations, driving up construction costs, and preventing the natural adjustments that would occur in a free market, zoning extracts an enormous economic toll that falls most heavily on young families, low-income workers, and those seeking to enter the housing market for the first time.

The relationship between zoning and housing costs is not coincidental but rather direct and substantial. Academic research consistently demonstrates that restrictive zoning regulations significantly increase housing prices. Studies of the San Francisco Bay Area, where some of the nation's most stringent zoning laws coincide with some of the nation's highest housing costs, reveal that regulatory constraints account for a substantial portion of the housing premium. Similarly, analyses of metropolitan areas across the country find that places with more restrictive zoning tend to have higher housing costs, larger homeless populations, and greater economic inequality. The mechanism is straightforward: when government limits what can be built and where it can be built, the supply of housing fails to keep pace with demand, and prices inevitably rise.

The impact on affordability extends far beyond the direct cost of housing. When workers cannot find affordable housing near employment centers, commuting times increase, transportation costs rise, and quality of life declines. The phenomenon of wealthy coastal cities with severe housing shortages while other regions have abundant affordable housing reflects not natural market forces but rather the artificial constraints that zoning imposes. Workers who would otherwise move to high-wage areas to seek better opportunities find themselves priced out, while employers in those areas struggle to find workers who can afford to live nearby. The economic inefficiency is vast and growing.

Abolishing zoning would unleash a construction boom that would dramatically improve housing affordability across the country. Developers, responding to market signals rather than bureaucratic constraints, would build the housing that people actually want and need. The artificial distinctions between residential, commercial, and industrial uses would disappear, allowing the organic development patterns that characterized successful cities before the zoning era. Houston, despite being the fourth-largest city in America, has no comprehensive zoning code—and far from resulting in urban chaos, it has developed into a vibrant metropolitan area with relatively affordable housing and diverse neighborhoods. The absence of zoning has not prevented Houston from functioning; rather, it has allowed the market to respond dynamically to changing conditions and preferences.

The construction industry would benefit enormously from zoning abolition, as would the broader economy. Removing regulatory barriers would reduce soft costs—the fees, delays, and design requirements that add substantially to the cost of new construction without providing corresponding benefits. In many jurisdictions, the approval process for new development takes years and involves numerous regulatory agencies, each with the power to impose additional requirements and delays. These processes benefit well-connected developers with the resources to navigate bureaucratic mazes while excluding smaller competitors and limiting the overall supply of new construction. Streamlining or eliminating these processes would increase competition, reduce costs, and expand opportunities for entrepreneurship in the construction sector.

Innovation, Adaptability, and Organic Development

Cities that developed organically before the zoning era display a vitality, diversity, and architectural interest that most contemporary developments lack. The historic neighborhoods of older American cities—with their mixed uses, varied building types, and human scale—demonstrate that market-driven development can create attractive, functional, and desirable communities. By contrast, the planned, zoned, and regulated developments of the post-zoning era often feel sterile, homogeneous, and disconnected from human needs and preferences.

The rigidity of zoning prevents adaptation to changing circumstances and preferences. As demographics shift, as technologies evolve, and as economic conditions change, communities must be able to evolve with them. Zoning freezes development patterns in place, preventing the organic adjustments that would otherwise occur. A neighborhood that was purely residential in 1950 may benefit from the addition of small shops, restaurants, and services as the population ages or as new residents seek walkable amenities—but zoning may prohibit such changes, condemning the neighborhood to stagnation or decline. Similarly, areas zoned for commercial or industrial use may become more valuable for residential purposes as cities evolve, but zoning prevents such conversions, locking in inefficient land-use patterns.

The prohibition on mixed-use development is particularly harmful, as it forces the rigid separation of residential, commercial, and industrial activities that the free market would naturally integrate. Humans have historically lived, worked, and traded in close proximity; the zoned city's radical separation of these functions is the historical anomaly, not the norm. The automobile-centric development patterns that zoning encourages—with vast suburban residential areas separated from commercial strips and industrial zones—impose enormous costs in terms of commuting time, transportation expenses, environmental damage, and community disconnection. A return to mixed-use, walkable development would reduce automobile dependence, strengthen local economies, and create more vibrant and interesting communities.

Innovation in architecture and urban design is stifled by the compliance requirements that zoning imposes. Creative architects and developers who might introduce new building types, construction methods, or community designs find themselves constrained by requirements for setbacks, height limits, lot coverage restrictions, and use prohibitions. The resulting built environment reflects not what people actually want but what regulators permit—often resulting in bland, homogeneous development that fails to inspire or delight. Removing these constraints would allow experimentation and innovation, potentially yielding new approaches to housing, commercial development, and community design that current regulations make impossible.

Environmental and Sustainability Benefits

Paradoxically, the complete abolition of zoning would likely produce environmental benefits that current regulatory approaches fail to achieve. The market mechanisms that would operate in the absence of zoning would naturally encourage denser, more efficient development patterns that reduce automobile dependence, preserve open space, and minimize the environmental impact of human settlement.

Current zoning often encourages low-density, automobile-dependent development by requiring large minimum lot sizes, mandating extensive setbacks, and separating residential areas from commercial services. This pattern sprawls development across the landscape, consuming farmland and natural areas, fragmenting ecosystems, and creating transportation systems that rely almost entirely on fossil fuels. The environmental consequences are severe: increased greenhouse gas emissions, air and water pollution, loss of biodiversity, and degradation of natural resources. Zoning thus contributes to environmental destruction even as it claims to protect environmental quality.

In a free market for land, by contrast, development would naturally concentrate in areas where the demand is highest, preserving more remote and environmentally sensitive areas from development. Rather than forcing uniform low-density development across vast areas, market-driven development would allow the efficient allocation of land to its highest and best use—which in many cases means denser development in urban cores and along transportation corridors, with surrounding lands left in agricultural or natural use. This pattern would preserve more open space overall while accommodating population growth in environmentally superior ways.

The market also provides superior mechanisms for addressing genuine environmental externalities. Rather than using zoning to dictate what can be built where, a property-rights-based approach would address pollution and environmental harm through tort liability, property rights enforcement, and pollution taxes or tradable permits. A factory that pollutes a river would be liable for damages to downstream property owners; a development that destroys wetland habitat would face claims from those harmed by the loss. These market-based mechanisms internalize environmental costs more effectively than zoning's blunt prohibitions, which often fail to address the actual sources of environmental harm while imposing substantial costs on legitimate development.

Addressing the NIMBY Objection

Critics of zoning abolition invariably raise the specter of NIMBYism—the "Not In My Backyard" phenomenon wherein existing residents oppose new development in their neighborhoods. Without zoning to serve as a legal barrier, the argument goes, developers would be free to build whatever they wanted wherever they wanted, and existing residents would have no protection against unwanted development. This objection deserves serious consideration, as it reflects genuine concerns about community character and the power of wealthy interests to overwhelm individual property owners.

However, this objection fundamentally misunderstands both the nature of property rights and the actual dynamics of development without zoning. In the first place, property owners already have substantial rights to control the use of their own land, and these rights include the ability to exclude others from their property. While zoning abolition would remove government-imposed barriers to development, it would not eliminate the market forces, private covenants, and community norms that shape development patterns. Developers who ignore community preferences find their projects unmarketable; neighborhoods that wish to maintain certain characteristics can create private mechanisms to do so, such as homeowners associations with enforceable design guidelines.

Furthermore, the NIMBY objection proves too much. If the fear is that developers will override community preferences without zoning, the logical response would be to strengthen private property rights and private ordering mechanisms, not to expand government zoning power. The current system empowers not communities but rather government bureaucracies and politically connected interests. In practice, zoning often serves to exclude rather than to protect—to prevent the construction of affordable housing, to maintain racial and economic segregation, and to preserve property values for wealthy homeowners at the expense of others. The supposedly community-protective function of zoning is in practice subverted to serve private interests, while genuine community input is channeled through adversarial public processes that favor organized opposition over organic development.

The proper response to legitimate concerns about development intensity, neighborhood character, and community preferences is not centralized government zoning but rather robust protection of property rights combined with private ordering mechanisms. Property owners who are harmed by neighboring development—through genuine externalities such as noise, pollution, or physical encroachment—already have recourse through tort law. Concerns about aesthetics and character are better addressed through private covenants and community associations than through government mandate. And concerns about the political power of developers are best addressed by reducing the stakes of government land-use decisions, which currently create enormous incentives for rent-seeking and corruption.

The Historical Anomaly of Zoning

A final consideration in favor of abolishing zoning is the recognition that comprehensive land-use regulation is a relatively recent historical development, unprecedented in human civilization before the twentieth century. Cities and communities functioned, thrived, and created architectural and urban wonders for thousands of years without the benefit of zoning codes. The great cities of history—the ancient cities of Greece and Rome, the medieval cities of Europe, the great cities of the Islamic world, the cities of pre-Columbian America—developed organically through market forces and private property rights, producing urban fabrics that continue to inspire admiration today.

The United States in particular developedremarkably without comprehensive zoning until the early twentieth century. The great American cities—Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Charleston, New Orleans—grew organically, with mixed uses, varied building types, and dense urban fabrics that remain among the country's most desirable neighborhoods. The architectural achievements of the nineteenth century—towering cathedrals, elegant mansions, functional warehouses, modest workers' housing—occurred entirely outside the zoning framework. The absence of zoning did not produce chaos; it produced the urban environments that today command premium prices and widespread admiration.

Zoning emerged in the early twentieth century not as a response to genuine market failures but as a tool of Progressive-era reformers who believed that expert planning could improve upon the apparently chaotic results of market-driven development. The early zoning movement was explicitly exclusionary, designed to protect wealthy neighborhoods from what were seen as the undesirable consequences of mixed-income, mixed-use development. Zoning in its origins was a tool of segregation and exclusion, and these origins continue to shape its operation today. The transition from explicit racial zoning to class-based zoning through minimum lot sizes, minimum house sizes, and restrictions on multifamily housing represents not a reform but a continuation of the same exclusionary impulse through different means.

The lesson of history is not that markets produce perfect outcomes—the free exchange of property rights produces development patterns that reflect the preferences and power of market participants, for better and worse. But the alternative—government planning—has produced its own failures, from the urban renewal disasters of the mid-twentieth century to the sterile, homogeneous suburban sprawl that characterizes much contemporary development. Given the choice between the organic vitality of market-driven development and the bureaucratic uniformity of planned development, history strongly favors the market.

Conclusion

The complete abolition of zoning laws represents not a radical experiment but a restoration—a return to the property rights and market freedom that characterized successful development throughout human history. The case for abolition rests on the most fundamental principles of a free society: the right of individuals to control their own property, the moral unacceptability of paternalistic government control, and the demonstrated capacity of free markets to produce prosperity and progress.

The economic benefits of zoning abolition are substantial and well-documented: increased housing supply, reduced housing costs, expanded economic opportunity, and more efficient land use. The social benefits are equally significant: the restoration of property rights, the reduction of government power over private decisions, and the empowerment of individuals to shape their own environments according to their own values and preferences. The environmental benefits, though often overlooked, are real: market-driven development would concentrate growth in appropriate areas, preserve open space, and reduce automobile dependence.

None of this is to claim that a world without zoning would be perfect. Markets can fail, property rights can be abused, and powerful interests can sometimes override legitimate concerns. But these problems exist under any system, and the proper responses to them lie in strengthening property rights, enforcing tort liability for genuine harms, and creating private mechanisms for community self-governance—not in expanding the bureaucratic apparatus of zoning that currently serves to exclude, to regulate, and to privilege the well-connected at the expense of everyone else.

The time has come to recognize zoning for what it is: an unconstitutional taking of property rights, an economic drag on prosperity, and an affront to human liberty. The solution is not reform but abolition. Let us return to the principle that property belongs to its owners, that markets are better planners than bureaucrats, and that freedom is the foundation of flourishing communities. Abolish zoning, and let liberty build the future.

Understanding the arguments for eliminating zoning entirely requires examining the theoretical foundations of property rights, the empirical evidence regarding housing markets, and the philosophical principles underlying free societies.

The Philosophical Foundation: Property Rights and Economic Liberty

The most fundamental argument for eliminating zoning laws rests on the principle that genuine property ownership must include the right to use one's property as one sees fit, subject only to prohibitions against direct harm to others. Under this view, when government tells a landowner that they cannot build a duplex on their lot, construct a building taller than thirty-five feet, operate a business from their home, or divide their property into smaller parcels, the government has effectively confiscated a portion of the value of that property without compensation. The property owner still holds legal title, but the economic utility and creative potential of that ownership has been substantially diminished by state decree.

This perspective draws on classical liberal and libertarian political philosophy, which holds that individuals possess natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that government exists primarily to protect these rights rather than to manage their exercise. From this standpoint, zoning laws represent a departure from the proper role of government. Rather than preventing genuine harms—such as pollution that drifts onto neighboring property, structures that collapse and injure passersby, or fraud in real estate transactions—zoning laws regulate the use of property based on aesthetic preferences, class-based assumptions about appropriate behavior, and visions of ideal community design that vary arbitrarily from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.

The economic implications of this philosophical stance are significant. When property rights are fully secure, owners have maximum incentive to invest in their property and to use it in ways that generate value for themselves and society. When those rights are contingent on compliance with extensive regulations that may change unpredictably, investment becomes more risky, underinvestment occurs, and the adaptive capacity of real estate markets is severely constrained. A homeowner who might otherwise add a secondary dwelling unit to house an aging parent or generate rental income instead faces a maze of permit requirements, public hearings, and uncertain approval processes. The result is not merely frustration for individual property owners but a systematic reduction in the productive capacity of the housing stock.

Housing Availability: Market Response to Regulatory Constraint

Perhaps the most tangible argument for eliminating zoning concerns the relationship between regulatory constraints and housing supply. Economic analysis consistently demonstrates that stringent land use regulations correlate strongly with reduced housing construction, concentrated development in already-dense areas, and higher housing costs. Houston, the only major American city without comprehensive zoning, has historically experienced more housing construction relative to population growth than comparable cities with extensive zoning codes, despite having no zoning restrictions whatsoever.

The mechanism through which zoning constrains housing supply operates on multiple levels. Most directly, minimum lot size requirements, density limits, and height restrictions cap the number of dwelling units that can be accommodated on a given parcel of land. When a city requires that single-family homes occupy lots of at least 7,500 square feet, it necessarily precludes the construction of denser housing types that could shelter more families on the same land area. This constraint becomes particularly consequential as cities grow and the demand for housing increases. If the underlying land base cannot accommodate additional units due to regulatory caps, then rising demand translates directly into rising prices rather than expanded supply.

Single-family zoning, which dominates residential land area in most American cities, represents perhaps the most significant constraint on housing availability. By prohibiting multi-family housing, townhouses, and accessory dwelling units in areas zoned for single-family detached homes, cities effectively reserve the majority of their land for a housing type that provides the least density per acre. As urban populations grow and demographic shifts increase demand for smaller households and rental housing, the prohibition on diverse housing types creates artificial scarcity in precisely those markets where demand is strongest.

Eliminating zoning would theoretically allow developers to respond to market signals by building the housing types that consumers actually want in the locations where they want them. When families prefer single-family homes with yards, developers could provide them. When young professionals prefer apartments in walkable neighborhoods, developers could provide those as well. When retirees want to downsize to smaller units while remaining in their established communities, they would not face regulatory barriers to constructing or purchasing appropriate housing. The market, freed from artificial constraints, would theoretically produce a housing stock that more closely matches the actual preferences and needs of the population.

Housing Affordability: The Cost of Regulatory Barriers

The connection between zoning deregulation and housing affordability represents one of the most thoroughly studied questions in urban economics, and the evidence consistently supports the view that restrictive zoning raises housing costs. Research examining housing prices across metropolitan areas has found that regions with more stringent land use regulations experience significantly higher housing costs even after controlling for income, climate, geography, and other factors that influence housing demand. This relationship persists across multiple studies employing different methodologies, suggesting a robust connection between regulatory burden and housing expense.

The economics underlying this relationship are straightforward. When regulatory barriers limit the supply of housing relative to demand, prices must rise to clear the market. A city that adds twenty thousand new households each year but permits construction of only fifteen thousand new units will experience upward pressure on prices regardless of the underlying health of its economy. The constrained supply forces buyers to compete more intensely for available units, bid up prices, and accept smaller or lower-quality housing than they might otherwise prefer. First-time homebuyers, low-income families, and young households are disproportionately harmed by this dynamic, as they have the least capacity to absorb price increases.

The costs of regulatory compliance represent another mechanism through which zoning raises housing prices. When developers must navigate extensive approval processes, hire consultants to prepare environmental impact reports, attend public hearings where neighbors may object to any change in their surroundings, and wait months or years for permits to be processed, these costs are ultimately passed on to homebuyers and renters. Studies have estimated that regulatory requirements add tens of thousands of dollars to the cost of each new home constructed in highly regulated markets. In high-cost regions such as the San Francisco Bay Area or New York metropolitan area, regulatory compliance costs may exceed one hundred thousand dollars per unit.

Eliminating zoning would, according to proponents of deregulation, dramatically reduce these compliance costs while simultaneously expanding the supply of buildable land. When developers can build by-right—meaning that approved plans can proceed immediately upon submission without discretionary review—the soft costs associated with extended approval processes disappear. When density restrictions are removed, projects that would otherwise be prohibited become viable, increasing competition for development opportunities and putting downward pressure on land prices. When a broader range of housing types can be built in a wider range of locations, housing can be produced closer to employment centers and existing infrastructure, reducing the transportation costs that contribute to total housing expense.

The affordability argument extends beyond new construction to the broader functioning of housing markets. When homeowners face restrictions on adding accessory dwelling units or converting their properties to rental use, the supply of rental housing remains artificially constrained. When zoning prohibits mixed-use development, residents must live in exclusively residential areas and travel to separate commercial areas for work, shopping, and services, increasing transportation costs and time burdens. When minimum lot sizes are large, the entry-level price for homeownership rises as buyers must purchase larger parcels than they may need or desire. Each of these constraints, while perhaps justified on grounds of neighborhood character or stability in isolation, collectively create a housing market that systematically serves the interests of existing property owners at the expense of those who would enter the market.

Property Rights and Democratic Accountability

Beyond the instrumental benefits of expanded housing supply and reduced costs, proponents of eliminating zoning argue that such deregulation would represent a restoration of fundamental property rights and a reorientation of land use decision-making toward more democratic and accountable processes. Current zoning regimes concentrate enormous power over land use in the hands of local government officials and appointed boards, whose decisions are often shaped by organized neighborhood groups, campaign contributors, and the preferences of existing residents rather than broader public interest.

The capture of zoning processes by NIMBY (Not In My Backyard) interests represents a significant concern for those who favor elimination of these regulations. When any development proposal requires public approval, those who benefit from the status quo—existing homeowners who may face competition from new construction—have strong incentives to participate in the approval process, while those who would benefit from new development—potential residents, young families, workers seeking housing near employment—are often unaware of specific proposals or unable to attend lengthy public hearings. The result is a systematic bias toward denial of development applications and maintenance of existing regulatory constraints.

Eliminating zoning would shift land use decisions from the realm of discretionary government approval to the realm of property rights and market exchange. Rather than requiring permits and public hearings, developers would be free to build whatever the market supports on land they own, subject only to generally applicable laws regarding building codes, nuisance, and property rights. Neighbors who believe a proposed development would harm them could seek redress through the courts under existing tort law rather than through the political process of zoning administration. This shift would not eliminate all conflict over land use but would restructure the terms of that conflict in ways that many argue are more consistent with principles of fairness and liberty.

The democratic accountability argument for eliminating zoning rests on the observation that current zoning regimes are remarkably stable and resistant to reform despite widespread recognition of their costs. Once a jurisdiction is zoned for single-family residential use, changing that designation to permit higher-density development faces opposition from affected property owners who benefit from the current arrangement. The political economy of zoning thus tends toward ever-more-restrictive regulation, as those who gain from restrictions organize effectively while those who pay the costs—future residents, housing consumers, the broader community—are dispersed and unorganized. Removing zoning from the political agenda entirely would, according to this view, prevent this dynamic from perpetuating and expanding regulatory constraints.

Addressing the Objections: What Happens Without Zoning

Critics of zoning elimination raise substantial concerns about potential negative consequences, and proponents have responded with theoretical arguments and empirical evidence addressing each objection. The concern that eliminating zoning would lead to chaotic, ugly, or incompatible development is addressed by pointing to the incentives of developers and property owners themselves. Developers who build structures that neighbors find objectionable may face reputational costs, reduced demand for their products, and difficulty assembling land for future projects. Property owners who maintain and improve their properties enhance their own value and that of surrounding land. The market provides incentives for compatible development even absent regulatory mandates.

The fear that industrial uses would locate next to residential areas is addressed by noting that property owners have strong incentives to avoid uses that would reduce the value of their property through noise, pollution, or other external harms. More fundamentally, nuisance law provides remedies for harms that do flow across property lines, so a factory emitting toxic fumes that damage neighboring property would remain liable for those harms regardless of zoning. The elimination of zoning would not eliminate the legal system for addressing genuine harms but would simply remove the prior regulatory constraint that prohibits certain uses regardless of whether they actually cause problems.

Concerns about infrastructure capacity—sewer systems, water supply, transportation networks—are addressed by noting that developers and property owners have incentives to ensure that their developments are served by adequate infrastructure and that markets already incorporate the costs of infrastructure extension and upgrade. Where infrastructure constraints genuinely bind, development will not occur regardless of zoning, but where infrastructure has capacity for additional development, preventing that development merely wastes the investment in infrastructure and raises costs for all users.

The argument that zoning ensures adequate provision of affordable housing is challenged by the empirical record. Despite decades of inclusionary zoning mandates, affordable housing requirements, and density bonuses, housing costs have risen most rapidly in jurisdictions with the most extensive affordable housing programs. The reason is straightforward: regulatory requirements add costs to development that are passed on to all consumers, and the affordable units that are produced represent a tiny fraction of the units that would be produced in an unregulated market. Eliminating regulatory constraints would expand total housing supply, and the resulting increase in overall housing availability would make housing more affordable across the income spectrum.

The Path Forward: Practical Considerations

While the theoretical case for eliminating zoning is relatively straightforward, the practical politics of deregulation present substantial challenges. Zoning has become deeply embedded in local government structures, professional planning practice, and public expectations over more than a century of application. Property owners have made investment decisions based on existing regulatory frameworks, and changes to those frameworks create winners and losers regardless of the direction of change.

Proponents of deregulation acknowledge these practical challenges while arguing that incremental approaches have proven insufficient. Sunset provisions that phase out zoning over defined periods, state-level preemption of local zoning authority, and judicial limitations on the scope of permissible land use regulation have all been proposed as mechanisms for achieving deregulation. The specific political strategy matters less, according to proponents, than the recognition that incremental reforms that leave the underlying zoning structure intact will continue to produce incremental results—namely, continued housing scarcity and continued infringement of property rights.

The case for eliminating zoning ultimately rests on the judgment that the current system imposes enormous costs on society—costs measured in housing affordability, economic opportunity, personal liberty, and democratic accountability—that are not justified by the benefits that zoning provides. When the philosophical commitment to property rights is combined with the empirical evidence on housing markets and regulatory effects, the argument for complete deregulation becomes compelling. Whether and how that deregulation might be achieved remains a question of political strategy, but the substantive case for ending zoning as a system of government control over land use has been thoroughly articulated and defended.

Dear Fellow Guardian of the Urban Landscape,

I write to you today from the trenches of civilization, where a new threat looms on the horizon. Savages—nay, anarchists—are demanding the complete abolition of zoning laws. These wild-eyed radicals want to build duplexes next to single-family homes. They want corner stores where children currently play. They dream, in their hallucinatory stupor, of mixed-use developments where people might actually walk to get groceries.

We cannot let this stand.

For too long, the forces of reason have remained silent while the barbarians at the gate insist that adults should be allowed to decide what to do with their own property. It's time we remind ourselves why the sacred institution of zoning exists—and why anyone who questions it is either dangerously naive or secretly plotting to destroy Western civilization as we know it.

But What About the Children?

Let's start with the most important argument, the one that trumps all others: the children. When someone proposes building an apartment complex, have they considered the children? They have not. They are monsters. Zoning laws exist, first and foremost, to protect children from having to see a building taller than their house. What if a child looked out their window and saw a four-story building? That child would be traumatized for life. We cannot risk this. The psychological literature is clear: children can only develop properly when their entire worldview consists of single-family homes arranged in curvilinear streets with cul-de-sacs they can ride their bikes in circles in, going absolutely nowhere, which is the whole point.

Speaking of which, have you considered the traffic? Of course you haven't. That's the thing about people who want to abolish zoning—they don't think. They just react with their hearts, those bleeding organs pumping empathy and common sense through their bodies like some sort of circulatory disease. If you let someone build a three-unit building, three families might move in. That's nine additional cars potentially on the road. Do you want your commute to take even longer than the ninety minutes it currently takes you to go four miles? Because this is how commutes get longer.

The Experts Agree (And by Experts, I Mean Us)

Supporters of zoning reform will tell you that housing costs are rising, that young people can't afford homes, that density reduces carbon emissions, and that cities function better when people can live near where they work. To this, I say: so what? These are merely data points, statistics, peer-reviewed studies, and economic analyses. Do you want to live in a world governed by numbers and evidence, or a world governed by values? I, for one, values the character of my neighborhood, which is defined entirely by the fact that every house looks exactly the same and nothing has changed since 1957, when my grandparents moved here and everything was perfect and will be perfect forever.

The great philosopher Jim Bakker once said, "Zoning is the architecture of the American Dream." I may have misattributed that quote, but the sentiment stands. Zoning isn't just about regulating land use—it's about regulating dreams. When a young couple wants to open a bakery in their garage, zoning laws are there to remind them: no. When an elderly widow wants to add a second unit to her home so she can afford to keep living there, zoning laws are there to tell her: absolutely not. When developers want to build anything other than a single-family home on a large plot of land, zoning laws are there to whisper a single, reassuring word: stop.

This is what freedom looks like.

A Brief History of Why We Can't Have Nice Things

Let's take a trip through history, shall we? In the old days—say, 1920—people could build whatever they wanted. And what did they build? Factories next to houses. Slaughterhouses next to schools. Textile mills that dumped their waste directly into rivers that children then played in. This was a disaster. Clearly, the solution was to create a comprehensive system of land-use regulations that would thoughtfully separate incompatible uses and create harmonious, functional communities.

But here's the thing: we didn't just separate the incompatible uses. We separated everything. We decided that houses should never be near stores, that stores should never be near offices, and that offices should never be near anything that might make them less profitable. We created suburbs, those monuments to human ingenuity where every meal requires a car trip and the average citizen spends four hours a week behind the wheel, communing with their thoughts and various podcasts about true crime.

And this was good. This was planned. Someone, somewhere, drew lines on a map, and by God, those lines have remained for seventy years because changing lines is hard and we are very tired.

The Zoning Apologist's Toolkit

Now, the zoning abolitionists will try to deceive you with their sophisticated rhetoric. They'll use phrases like "housing affordability," "transit-oriented development," and "missing middle housing." They'll show you pictures of walkable neighborhoods in Europe where people live to be 100 years old because they walk everywhere and encounter actual human beings during their daily routines. They'll try to tell you that Houston, despite having no zoning, hasn't descended into chaos.

Don't fall for it.

These people are tricksters, conjurers oflogic, peddlers of reason. They want you to think that the rules governing what you can do with your property are arbitrary obstacles erected by powerful interests to protect their investments rather than tools of good planning. They want you to believe that if someone wants to build an accessory dwelling unit on their property, the primary barrier isn't a 200-page manual of regulations, public hearings, and a board that meets once every six weeks to consider applications.

They want you to think that you, a free adult, should be able to decide what to do with the land you own.

This is, frankly, un-American.

A Modest Proposal

I have a solution that will satisfy everyone. Instead of abolishing zoning laws, let's expand them. Why should zoning only apply to residential and commercial areas? Let's zone everything. At what hours are you allowed to wake up? Zoning will determine that. What are you permitted to dream about? Zoning has you covered. How many children are you allowed to have? The Comprehensive Plan addresses this in Appendix J, Table 4.3.

We could create a society of perfect predictability, where nothing ever changes and every outcome is optimized for the median preferences of people who attended Planning Board meetings in 1987. Is this stifling? Perhaps. But it's the kind of stifling that creates stability, the kind of stability that comes from knowing your neighborhood will never, ever improve in any way that might make you uncomfortable.

Conclusion: The Horror of Choice

The real problem with abolishing zoning is that it would force us to confront an uncomfortable truth: that the world is complex, that different people have different needs, that communities can evolve organically, and that perhaps—just perhaps—local residents acting in their own self-interest might create functional neighborhoods without the guiding hand of municipal bureaucracy.

That's terrifying. That's chaos. That's the road to ruin.

When I close my eyes at night, I don't see vibrant, mixed-use communities where people of diverse incomes and backgrounds interact naturally. I see the inferno described by zoning abolitionists: a world where someone might build a duplex next door to my house, and I would have to talk to my neighbors, and they might be different from me, and we might have to work out our differences like civilized people instead of hiding behind regulatory barriers designed to enforce homogeneity.

I can't bear it.

Save us, zoning laws. Save us from ourselves.
